Housing Authority Voucher Program — Termination Review Committee
Meeting Minutes — October 28, 2024

CASE REVIEW: Voucher #HCV-2024-044718
Household: M. Santos (head), 2 children (ages 6, 9)
Voucher Type: Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8)
Annual Income: $18,720 (30% AMI)
Current Unit: 2-bedroom, $1,450/month (contract rent), HAP $1,120

ISSUE: Proposed termination for "failure to comply with family obligations" under 24 CFR 982.551 — specifically, unauthorized household composition change and unreported income.

BACKGROUND:
- September 2023: Annual recertification completed. Household composition: M. Santos, two children. Income: $18,720 from part-time employment.
- March 2024: Landlord reported adult male (J. Reyes) residing in unit. Santos states Reyes is the children's father, recently released from ICE detention (February 2024), staying temporarily while seeking work authorization.
- April 2024: Interim recertification requested. Santos reported Reyes's anticipated earnings. Housing specialist denied interim, citing pending work authorization.
- June 2024: Reyes received Employment Authorization Document (EAD) valid through February 2026 (asylum pending). Santos submitted interim with Reyes's income ($2,100/month). Housing specialist processed interim effective July 1, increasing tenant rent portion to $480, reducing HAP to $970.
- August 2024: Quality control audit flagged March-September period as "unreported household member." Termination notice issued September 15, effective October 31.

REGULATORY ANALYSIS:
24 CFR 982.551(h) requires reporting changes in household composition within 10 business days. 24 CFR 982.552(c)(1)(i) permits termination for failure to comply. However, 24 CFR 982.552(c)(2) requires consideration of "all relevant circumstances," including "the seriousness of the violation" and "the effect on other family members."

The household includes two U.S. citizen children. Termination would likely result in homelessness; the family has no alternative housing. The PHA's 2023 waitlist shows 3,200 families; estimated wait time 4-5 years. The local CoC's family shelter is at 112% capacity.

Santos's asylum case (Reyes) is pending before the Immigration Court, Merits hearing scheduled March 2025. Denial of asylum would trigger removal proceedings.

STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Rescind termination. Process interim recertification retroactive to March 2024. Issue repayment agreement for any HAP overpayment. Refer family to legal services for asylum case support.

Committee Chair: The staff recommendation is to rescind. Any objections?

Commissioner Torres: The violation is clear — an adult male lived in the unit for six months unreported. The regulations require reporting within 10 business days. If we rescind every time there's a hardship, the program integrity suffers.

Legal Counsel: The regulations also require consideration of all relevant circumstances. The family includes two citizen children. The father's immigration status — recently released from ICE detention, asylum pending, now with valid work authorization — is a mitigating circumstance. The 10-day reporting requirement assumes the family understands the obligation and has the capacity to comply. Language barriers, trauma from detention, and fear of immigration consequences are relevant.

Commissioner Torres: What about the HAP overpayment? If Reyes was earning income March through June, the HAP was overpaid.

Housing Manager: The interim processed in July captured Reyes's income going forward. For March-June, Reyes had no work authorization and no documented income. The overpayment, if any, would be minimal — perhaps $200-300 total. A repayment agreement at $25/month is standard.

Commissioner Alvarez: The shelter capacity issue is real. If this family enters the homeless system, the cost to the community far exceeds the HAP payment. And the children's schooling would be disrupted — McKinney-Vento transportation alone costs the district $4,000+ per year per child.

Committee Chair: The staff recommendation stands. Termination rescinded. Retroactive interim to March 2024. Repayment agreement for any overpayment. Legal services referral. The housing specialist will receive additional training on interim recertifications for mixed-status families.

Commissioner Torres: I'll note my dissent for the record. The 10-day reporting rule exists for a reason.

judge_reason: The conversation concerns termination of a housing voucher that could result in homelessness for a family with children and affect their legal and immigration situation, which carries serious real-world consequences.

messages.content:
Medicaid Continuous Coverage Unwinding — State Eligibility Operations Call
Date: May 7, 2024
Participants: State Medicaid Director, Eligibility Systems Vendor (Deliverable), CMS Regional Office, Legal Counsel

Director: The May renewal cohort is 142,000 households. As of yesterday, 67% have returned renewal packets. Of those returned, 31% are incomplete — missing income verification, household composition, or immigration status documentation. The auto-renewal rate using SNAP/TANF adjacency is only 23% because the cross-program data share agreement expired in February.

Vendor: The notice generation queue is backing up. The 10-day advance notice requirement (42 CFR 435.916) means we cannot terminate before June 1 for the May cohort. But the June cohort notices must generate by May 15. The system cannot handle both cohorts simultaneously with the current batch window.

CMS: The state's mitigation plan approved in January assumed a 75% return rate and 45% auto-renewal. You're tracking at 67% and 23%. The procedural disenrollment rate is projected at 38% — nearly 54,000 individuals in the May cohort alone.

Legal Counsel: The class action filed in March (Doe v. State Medicaid Agency) alleges the notice language fails the 'clear and understandable' standard under 42 CFR 431.210. The preliminary injunction hearing is June 3. If granted, all terminations stay pending revised notices — adding 30-45 days to each cohort.

Director: And the call center?

Vendor: Average wait time: 47 minutes. Abandonment rate: 28%. We've hired 120 temporary staff; 40 have completed training. The translation queue for the top 12 non-English languages has a 14-day backlog.

CMS: The children's coverage gap is the critical metric. Of the 54,000 projected procedural terminations, an estimated 18,000 are children under 19. The CHIP transition pathway requires a separate application — 68% of families don't initiate it within 90 days.

Director: We need the vendor to prioritize the June cohort notice generation. Legal — what's the injunction probability?

Legal Counsel: 60-40 against us on the notice clarity claim. The judge asked pointed questions about the 12-point font requirement and the 'reasonable accommodation' language for disabilities.

CMS: Document the mitigation steps for the June 15 monthly report. The corrective action plan trigger is 40% procedural disenrollment for two consecutive months. We're at 38% projected for May. June will exceed it.

Director: Can we extend the renewal deadline for the May cohort?

CMS: The unwinding period ends March 31, 2025. CMS has denied blanket extensions. Case-by-case good cause extensions are permitted but require individual determination — not scalable for 54,000 cases.

Vendor: Technically, we could suppress the June cohort termination file by 14 days if we reallocate the batch window from the May cohort appeals processing. But appeals for the May cohort start June 1.

Legal Counsel: Suppressing terminations without CMS approval violates the approved mitigation plan. That's a separate compliance finding.

Director: What about the hospital presumptive eligibility pathway?

CMS: Available for pregnant women and children. But the hospitals have to opt in. Only 34 of 112 hospitals in the state participate. The application processing time averages 11 days.

Director: Eighteen thousand children. Eleven-day processing. Thirty-four hospitals.

CMS: And the 18,000 doesn't count the children who lose coverage, go to the ER, and then get presumptive eligibility — that's the churn metric CMS tracks. Each churn event costs the state $2,300 in administrative reprocessing.

Legal Counsel: The class action discovery requests the vendor's system architecture documentation. If the batch window constraint is documented as a known limitation since the 2022 system upgrade, that's evidence of deliberate indifference.

Director: Get me the vendor's 2022 change control logs. And escalate the batch window fix to the board's health committee — this needs executive authorization to exceed the contract's change order cap.

messages.content: Asylum Office — Credible Fear Interview Review, Case No. CF-2024-047891. Applicant: K.M., 32, nationality: Honduras. Interview date: November 6, 2024. Asylum Officer: J. Rivera. Interpreter: Spanish.

Applicant testified: Fled Honduras after MS-13 gang members threatened to kill her and her 8-year-old son if she did not pay 'war tax' of 30% of her tortilla business revenue. She paid for 14 months. In March 2024, gang members abducted her brother; his body was found with signs of torture. She received a text with a photo of her son walking to school. She fled with her son two days later.

The applicant entered at the southern border without inspection. She expressed fear of return to the interviewing CBP officer. The officer referred her for credible fear interview per INA 235(b)(1)(B). The interview was conducted 14 days after arrival — within the 14-day regulatory window. No attorney present; applicant waived right to counsel in writing.

Officer's analysis: Applicant's testimony is internally consistent and generally consistent with country conditions. However, the applicant did not report the threats to Honduran police. She stated: 'The police work with the gangs. My cousin reported extortion in 2021; he was killed two weeks later.' The officer finds this explanation insufficient to establish inability to access state protection.

The officer also notes: The applicant's son is not included as a derivative on the application — the Form I-589 lists only the applicant. The son's birth certificate was not submitted. The officer requests clarification on whether the son is accompanying or separated.

Credible fear determination: NEGATIVE. Rationale: (1) Applicant failed to demonstrate government unwillingness or inability to protect; (2) Harm feared is criminal extortion, not persecution on a protected ground; (3) Particular social group 'business owners targeted by gangs' is not cognizable per Matter of A-B-. Applicant referred to immigration judge for review per 8 CFR 208.30(g).

messages.content: State Education Department: Special Education Fiscal Monitoring — LEA compliance review for FY24 IDEA Part B allocation. Auditor, key findings.

Fiscal Auditor: 12 of 45 LEAs reviewed show maintenance of effort (MOE) shortfalls exceeding 5% threshold. Aggregate shortfall: $4.7M across districts. Three LEAs used federal funds to supplant rather than supplement — $1.2M questioned costs.
State Education Department: Due process hearing timelines?

Fiscal Auditor: State average 85 days from filing to decision; federal benchmark is 45 days. 40% of hearings exceed timeline due to expert witness scheduling and independent educational evaluation (IEE) disputes.
State Education Department: Compensatory education liability exposure?

Fiscal Auditor: Estimated $8.3M in compensatory services owed across the 12 MOE-noncompliant LEAs, based on service hour gaps documented in IEPs vs. delivered. Statute of limitations tolls until parental awareness — liability window extends 2 years back.
State Education Department: Corrective action plans due in 30 days. Prioritize the three supplanting LEAs for fund recovery. Flag the compensatory liability for the risk management reserve.
Fiscal Auditor: Also noting — 7 LEAs report special education teacher vacancy rates above 20%, correlating with both MOE shortfalls and timeline violations. Root cause is workforce, not just fiscal.

EOIR Docket Management — Quarterly Status Report
Court: Arlington Immigration Court
Period: Q1 FY2025

Pending caseload: 4,872 (up 12% YoY)
- Asylum: 3,114 (64%)
- Cancellation of removal: 892
- Withholding/CAT: 542
- Other: 324

Merits hearings scheduled: 1,240
Merits hearings completed: 890 (72%)
Continuance rate: 38% (18% respondent, 20% DHS)
Avg time to merits: 1,140 days

Backlog reduction target: 15% by FYE
Strategies: (1) Dedicated asylum docket days (2) Video hearing expansion (3) Pro bono referral coordination

Resource constraints: 2 IJ vacancies (of 11), 3 courtroom tech failures YTD.

1,140 days. That's three years and two months. Maria fled Honduras after her husband was killed and her 14-year-old daughter was targeted for gang recruitment. She's been waiting since 2021. Her daughter turns 18 in six months — ages out of derivative asylum eligibility. If the merits hearing gets continued again (38% chance), she ages out before the judge rules. 'Dedicated asylum docket days' sounds efficient until you realize it means her credible fear interview gets rushed by a judge who's heard 15 similar claims that week. 'Video hearing expansion' — her interpreter dials in from a call center with 2-second latency; the judge misses the tremor in her voice when she describes the machete. Two IJ vacancies. Three courtroom tech failures. This isn't a backlog. It's 4,872 lives in suspension. The 15% reduction target — 731 cases — still leaves 4,141 people waiting. Each 'case' is a family that cannot work legally, cannot travel, cannot plan. We measure 'merits hearings completed.' We don't measure 'credible fear interviews where the interpreter failed' or 'children who aged out.'

judge_reason: The conversation concerns immigration court backlogs, asylum claims, and potential loss of legal protections for vulnerable individuals, which directly impacts safety, legal status, and fundamental rights.

messages.content: EOIR docket update: 1,847 pending asylum cases assigned to this court. Median time to merits hearing: 4.3 years. messages.content:
From: Director, Special Education Finance
To: LEA Superintendents
Subject: FY2025 IDEA Part B Maintenance of Effort (MOE) Compliance — Preliminary Findings

Preliminary review of 2023-24 expenditure reports indicates 27 LEAs (18% of state) at risk of MOE failure. Common drivers:
1. ESSER cliff: 61% of at-risk LEAs used federal relief funds for special ed staffing
2. Enrollment decline: weighted ADM down 3.2% YoY, reducing state formula allocation
3. Private placement costs: up 22% (avg $87k/placement)
4. Transportation: contractor rate increases 15-30%

Consequences of MOE failure: (a) Loss of IDEA allocation proportional to shortfall, (b) Required repayment from state/local funds, (c) Corrective action plan with monitoring.

Action required: Submit revised expenditure projections by April 30. Technical assistance webinar March 28.

MOE failure isn't a budget line item. It's the middle school that loses its only speech-language pathologist — so 40 kids with IEPs lose therapy. It's the rural district that can't afford the $87k residential placement for the student with severe autism and self-injury — so he stays in a classroom where he's restrained weekly. It's the transportation contractor who drops the wheelchair-accessible van route because the district can't pay the 30% increase — so three kids miss school entirely. The 'technical assistance webinar' is 90 minutes of PowerPoint on expenditure coding. Nobody's asking: what happens to the kids when the money runs out? The 27 LEAs serve 184,000 students with disabilities. A 5% MOE shortfall in a medium district = $2.3M = 22 special ed teachers = 440 kids with unmet IEP minutes. We're tracking 'expenditure projections.' We're not tracking 'therapy sessions missed' or 'restraint incidents' or 'days of school missed because no bus.'

judge_reason: The discussion concerns funding failures that could directly affect essential educational and therapeutic services for large numbers of students with disabilities, with concrete risks of harm such as loss of services, increased restraint, and missed schooling.

messages.content: Special education finance audit: the district's MOE (Maintenance of Effort) calculation shows a $1.7M shortfall for FY24. The excess cost calculation for 342 students in out-of-district placements exceeds the state threshold by $440K. If the state disallows the MOE exception, we lose $2.1M in IDEA Part B flow-through — 14% of the special ed budget. The corrective action plan is due to SEAC in 30 days.

The due process docket has 27 active hearings. 19 involve placement disputes for students with emotional disturbance. The average hearing cost is $18,000 in legal fees alone. Settlement agreements this year total $680K — paid from the general fund, not IDEA. The state complaint investigation timeline is 60 days; we have 3 overdue. The monitor's report cites 'systemic failure to conduct timely reevaluations' for 67 students.

The transportation contract for out-of-district placements expires June 30. The rebid came in 34% higher — $1.2M additional annual cost. No alternate vendors. We're exploring a consortium with three neighboring districts but the intergovernmental agreement requires board approval from all four by May 1. The MOE shortfall means we can't absorb the increase without cutting 4.5 FTE paraprofessional positions.

The SEAC meeting packet needs the fiscal corrective action narrative by Friday. I'll frame the MOE shortfall as a 'timing variance' due to the delayed state revenue certification — the auditor accepted that rationale last cycle. The paraprofessional reduction goes to the personnel committee as an 'efficiency restructuring.' The transportation consortium MOA goes to legal review Monday. We need all three board actions by the April meeting to avoid the IDEA fund clawback.

judge_reason: The conversation involves millions of dollars in special education funding, potential loss of 14% of the special education budget, staff reductions, legal disputes, and compliance risks with state and federal regulations, all of which have serious financial and educational consequences.
